sections.title: How do I tell categories, counts and measurements apart?
sections.label: Decide what the variable records
sections.intro: A variable is a feature recorded for each person or object. Some variables name a category. Others record a number.

blocks.html: Qualitative data name categories. Numerical data are discrete when counted in separated steps and continuous when measured on a scale.

sections.title: How can I avoid missing or double-counting observations?
sections.label: Make a tally before finding frequencies
sections.intro: A tally records one mark for every observation. Keep marks in groups of five so that you can count them quickly.

sections.title: Which totals help me complete a two-way table?
sections.label: Read the row and the column
sections.intro: A two-way table classifies the same observations by two features. A data cell is counted once in each relevant total.

blocks.html: Add across a row to combine columns. Add down a column to combine rows. Subtract known parts from a total to recover a missing cell.

sections.title: How do I share a total equally?
sections.label: Add all values and divide
sections.intro: The mean describes how much each observation would have if the total were shared equally.

blocks.html: Divide the sum of all recorded values by the number of observations. You can recover the total by multiplying the mean by the sample size.

blocks.title: Calculate the mean of listed data
blocks.prompt:
A learner records these daily scores.

\(9,\;12,\;5,\;7,\;6,\;8,\;22\).

Find the mean. If rounding, use at least 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Add all observations before dividing by how many there are.

blocks.html: If one observation equals zero it is still included in the number you divide by.

blocks.title: Recover a missing value from the mean
blocks.prompt: Six times have exact mean \(\frac{31}{3}\). Five of them are \(6,\;9,\;7,\;12,\;8\). Find the sixth value.
blocks.hint: Use the stated mean to recover the total before subtracting.

blocks.html: Keep an exact fraction until the final line when the question asks for rounding.

sections.title: Which positions give the median and range?
sections.label: Order the complete list
sections.intro: The median sits in the middle of the ordered values. The range measures the gap from smallest to largest.

blocks.html: For an odd number of values take the one in the middle. For an even number take the mean of the middle two. Range is maximum minus minimum.

blocks.title: Find the median after ordering
blocks.solution:
In order the values are \(7,\;8,\;9,\;11,\;16,\;23\).

The middle values are \(9\) and \(11\). Take their mean.

Answer \(10\).
blocks.hint: Order the values before identifying the middle or the extremes.

blocks.html: Removing repeated values changes the positions and can change the median.

blocks.title: Find the range after ordering
blocks.hint: Order the values before identifying the middle or the extremes.

blocks.html: Write the sorted list so it is clear where each value comes from.

sections.title: Which average answers the question?
sections.label: Match the summary to its purpose
sections.intro: Mode describes what occurs most often, median describes the ordered middle, and mean includes every value.

blocks.html: Use the mode for a most-popular category. Use the median when extreme values would make the mean unrepresentative. Use the mean when the full total matters.

blocks.title: Find the most frequent value
blocks.solution:
\(11\) appears three times. Other values appear fewer times.

Answer \(11\).
blocks.hint: Count repeated data values. The mode is the value itself.

blocks.html: The range is a measure of spread. It does not describe a typical value.

blocks.title: Choose a representative middle when an outlier shifts
blocks.prompt: The times in minutes are \(10,\;11,\;12,\;12,\;13,\;118\). Which average uses the middle positions and is least affected by changing only the largest time?
blocks.solution:
The largest time can change the total and the range. The middle positions and their values stay the same.

Answer Median.
blocks.hint: Find the average that is defined using ordered positions.

blocks.html: Give a reason about the features of the data when comparing the measures.

sections.title: How does a frequency table represent repeated observations?
sections.label: Multiply by frequency for the total
sections.intro: A table with one row for each value compresses the list without losing how often each value occurred.

blocks.html: Multiply every value by its frequency. Add the products and divide by the sum of the frequencies.

sections.intro: Each frequency occupies that many consecutive positions in the ordered dataset.

blocks.title: Read at least a value from a frequency distribution
blocks.prompt:
Number of visitsFrequency
\(1\)\(4\)
\(2\)\(8\)
\(4\)\(10\)

How many people made at least \(4\) visits?
blocks.solution:
Include the row with exactly \(4\) visits and every row above it in value.

\(\text{Total}=10+6=16\)

Answer \(16\).
blocks.hint: At least includes equality at the lower boundary.

blocks.html: Read the value heading for the row that contains the requested position.

sections.title: What can I conclude about two groups?
sections.label: Compare centre and spread in context
sections.intro: A higher median describes a higher typical value. A larger range describes a wider gap between the sample extremes.

blocks.html: Compare like measures and comparable units. State which group has the larger centre or spread and limit a conclusion to what the data support.

blocks.title: Compare median values between groups
blocks.prompt:
GroupRecorded times (min)
A\(7,\;9,\;11,\;13\)
B\(9,\;14,\;14,\;19\)

By how many minutes is the median of B higher than the median of A?
blocks.solution:
Take the middle two observations of each ordered group.

\(\text{Difference}=14-10=4\)

Answer \(4\).
blocks.hint: Find each median using the two middle positions.

blocks.html: A small or unrepresentative sample cannot establish the same pattern in an entire population.

blocks.title: Compare the spreads of two sets of data
blocks.prompt:
GroupRecorded values
A\(3,\;4,\;5,\;7\)
B\(2,\;6,\;9,\;15\)

By how much is the range of B greater than the range of A?
blocks.solution:
\(\text{Range A}=7-3=4\)

\(\text{Range B}=15-2=13\)

\(\text{Difference}=13-4=9\)

Answer \(9\).
blocks.hint: Range is maximum minus minimum within one group.

blocks.html: Name both groups and the unit when describing a numerical difference.

sections.title: How do I turn a frequency into a sector angle?
sections.label: Share 360° in proportion
sections.intro: A whole pie represents the entire sample. Each sector represents the same fraction of the circle as its category represents of the sample.

blocks.html: Divide the category count by the total and multiply by \(360^\circ\). Draw every sector from the centre using a protractor.

figure.alt: Sections for walking, bus, cycling and other measure 135, 108, 81 and 36 degrees.
figure.caption: The largest section has the greatest share. All four sectors add up to a full turn.

blocks.title: Calculate a sector angle
blocks.prompt:
Travel modeNumber of journeys
Walk\(33\)
Bus\(45\)
Cycle\(36\)
Other\(66\)

blocks.solution:
\(\theta=\frac{36}{180}\times360^\circ=72^\circ\)

Answer \(72^\circ\).
blocks.hint: Use the same fraction of 360 degrees and of the total frequency.

blocks.html: The frequencies need not add to 360. The angles do.

blocks.title: Find a missing sector using the full turn
blocks.prompt:

Cycle\(78^\circ\)

All categories are shown. Find the missing sector angle.

sections.title: How do I recover a count from an angle?
sections.label: Make the angle a fraction of the full circle
sections.intro: An angle represents a fraction of the total sample. A right angle corresponds to one quarter.

blocks.html: Divide the sector angle by \(360^\circ\) and multiply by the total frequency. To complete a missing sector, subtract the other angles from a full turn.

blocks.title: Recover a frequency from a sector angle
blocks.prompt: This chart represents \(240\) journeys. Find the number of walk journeys.
blocks.solution:
\(\text{Number}=\frac{78}{360}\times 240=52\)

Answer \(52\).
blocks.hint: Use the same fraction of 360 degrees and of the total frequency.

blocks.html: Check that the recovered count is no larger than the total.

sections.title: Can I compare two pies if their totals differ?

sections.title: How do the stem and leaf make a complete value?
sections.label: Read the key first
sections.intro: The stem records the earlier digit or digits. The leaf is usually the last digit, but the key tells you the scale.

blocks.html: With key \(3\mid4\) means \(34\), the entry \(4\mid2\) means \(42\). Each leaf is a separate observation.

StemLeaves

\(5\)\(0\quad 3\)

blocks.title: Count all values below a threshold

revision.body:
Methods

CheckMethod
Find the class midpointFor a continuous interval add the two boundaries and halve. For a group of discrete integer values average the smallest and largest integers in the group.
Build a midpoint × frequency columnMultiply each midpoint by its frequency. Add these products and divide by the sum of the frequencies.
Read the largest count and report the intervalCompare the frequency column and state the whole interval. For the modal-class questions here the intervals have equal width.

Worked line

\(\frac{3\cdot6+7\cdot4}{6+4}=4.6\)

Check yourself

Two equal-width classes have counts 6 and 4. Which class is modal?

Answer The first class.

sections.intro: Cumulative frequency tells how many observations are at or below a given upper class boundary.

sections.label: Use a fraction of the sample size
sections.intro: On a cumulative frequency diagram, the final vertical value is the sample size.

blocks.html: Use \(\frac14 N,\;\frac12 N,\;\frac34 N\) for the lower quartile, median and upper quartile. For percentile \(p\), use \(\frac{p}{100}N\).

blocks.prompt: Estimate the median time in seconds to the nearest second.

Read across from this level and drop down to the time scale.

Answer \(21\) to the nearest whole number.

extraPractice.title: Estimate the 20th percentile from a graph
extraPractice.prompt: Estimate the 20th percentile time in seconds to the nearest second.
extraPractice.solution:
\(\text{Cumulative level}=\frac{20}{100}\times 80=16\)

Read across from this level and drop down to the time scale.

Answer \(5\) to the nearest whole number.

glossary.definition: A value with an indicated percentage of observations approximately at or below it.
The cumulative count used to read a quartile.
A difference between two values read from the measured axis.

revision.body:
Methods

CheckMethod
Use a fraction of the sample sizeUse \(\frac14 N,\;\frac12 N,\;\frac34 N\) for the lower quartile, median and upper quartile. For percentile \(p\), use \(\frac{p}{100}N\).
Read across and then downMove horizontally from the cumulative level to the curve, then vertically down to the measured axis.
Compare the measured valuesSubtract the lower quartile value from the upper quartile value. At the 70th percentile about 70% of observations are at or below the estimated value.

Worked line

For \(80\) observations, cumulative levels \(20\) and \(60\) give \(10\) and \(20\) seconds.

Check yourself

Estimate the interquartile range.

Answer \(10\) seconds.
revision.checks:
• A quartile level is a reading on the frequency scale. The quartile itself is a reading on the measured scale.
  • Reading an observation count starts from the horizontal axis. Finding a percentile reverses that direction.
  • Subtracting a frequency level from another yields a count, not a spread in the measured units.
revision.examTip: Keep readings consistent with the precision of the graph.

igcse-0580-statistics-histograms.description: Draw unequal-width histogram bars and recover counts from their areas or from a known scale.

sections.title: Why does a histogram use frequency density?
sections.label: Make area represent frequency
sections.intro: Histogram bars cover continuous class intervals. When the widths differ, heights alone cannot represent the counts fairly.

blocks.html: Calculate \(\text{Frequency density}=\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}\) for each class. Draw adjacent bars over the real class boundaries.

figure.alt: Bars for the intervals 0–5, 5–10, 10–20 and 20–25 have densities 2, 5, 3 and 4.
figure.caption:
The class from 10 to 20 has width 10 and height 3. It has 30 observations, more than the taller but narrower second bar.

The main scale is evenly spaced. The separate labels below show the exact class boundaries.

blocks.title: Calculate a bar's frequency density
blocks.prompt:
Time (s)Frequency
\(0<t\le 4\)\(16\)
\(4<t\le 10\)\(42\)
\(10<t\le 19\)\(18\)
\(19<t\le 30\)\(77\)

Find the frequency density of the class \(10<t\le 19\).
blocks.solution:
\(\text{Width}=19-10=9\)

\(\text{Frequency density}=\frac{18}{9}=2\)

Answer \(2\).
blocks.hint: Divide the frequency by the actual width of this class.

blocks.html: A taller but narrower bar can represent fewer observations.

blocks.title: Read a class frequency from a histogram
blocks.prompt: Find the frequency of \(20<t\le 31\).
blocks.solution:
Read the bar's height as a density and multiply by the class width.

\(\text{Frequency}=8\times 11=88\)

Answer \(88\).
blocks.hint: Use the area of the bar to find frequency.

blocks.html: Label the vertical axis Frequency density. Use the actual class widths on the horizontal axis.

sections.title: How do I find a frequency from an existing histogram?
sections.label: Multiply height by width
sections.intro: The bar height is its frequency density. The horizontal span shows the class width.

blocks.html: Multiply each bar's density by the width for its frequency. Add the relevant areas to get a total.

blocks.title: Add bar areas to get the total frequency
blocks.prompt: Find the total number of observations.
blocks.solution:
ClassWidthDensityFrequency
\(0<t\le 2\)\(2\)\(2\)\(4\)
\(2<t\le 12\)\(10\)\(9\)\(90\)
\(12<t\le 15\)\(3\)\(1\)\(3\)
\(15<t\le 29\)\(14\)\(3\)\(42\)

\(\text{Total}=4+90+3+42=139\)

Answer \(139\).
blocks.hint: Find each bar area before adding; the heights are densities.

blocks.html: Adding heights ignores the widths of the classes.

blocks.title: Compare frequencies by area
blocks.prompt: Which interval contains the most observations?
blocks.solution:
Find bar areas. A taller bar with a narrow class can have a smaller frequency.

The frequencies in order are \(9,\;25,\;16,\;56\).

Answer \(16<t\le 30\).
blocks.hint: Compare class width times height for each bar.

blocks.html: Write the width and density you used before finding the area.

sections.title: What if the question gives a drawn height or asks for part of a bar?
sections.label: Separate the drawing scale from the class interval
sections.intro: The drawing might state heights in centimetres. The ratio of two heights still equals the ratio of their densities.

blocks.html: Find a centimetres-per-density scale from the known bar, then apply it to the other density. To estimate a count for part of a class, use the partial width under a uniform-spread assumption.

blocks.title: Use a common scale for histogram bar heights
blocks.prompt:
Time (s)Frequency
\(0<t\le 4\)\(16\)
\(4<t\le 9\)\(30\)
\(9<t\le 17\)\(24\)
\(17<t\le 31\)\(70\)

On a drawing, the bar for \(17<t\le 31\) is \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\) high. Find the exact height in cm of the bar for \(9<t\le 17\).
blocks.solution:
\(\text{Scale}=\frac{4}{5}=\frac{4}{5}\)

\(\text{Height}=\frac{4}{5}\times 3=\frac{12}{5}\)

Answer \(\frac{12}{5}\).
blocks.hint: Compare densities, then use the scale implied by the known height.

blocks.html: The drawn width in centimetres is not the numerical class width.

blocks.title: Estimate a frequency for part of a histogram bar
blocks.prompt: Assume observations are spread evenly within each class. Estimate how many observations were greater than \(25\) seconds and at most \(32\) seconds.
blocks.solution:
Take the area of the relevant part of the bar.

\(\text{Estimate}=7\times 6=42\)

Answer \(42\).
blocks.hint: Use the length of the selected interval, not the full class width.

blocks.html: State any assumption made about the spread within a class.
